items.title: Introduction
items.text:
Utilities library for working with strings.

Simply install this amazing utilities package:

uv add stringz

And immediately get the benefits

from stringz import pretty_str, ding

result = pretty_str("Hello world!", max_chars=10)
print(result)  # Output: 'Hello w...'

items.title: Installation
items.text:
pipuv 
pip install stringz

uv add stringz

Requires Python 3.12+. Supported on Windows, macOS, Linux.

items.title: trunc_str
items.text:
trunc_str(text, max_chars, placeholder='...')

A function that truncates a string to a maximum number of characters, appending a placeholder if truncation occurs.

Example

Basic usage:

from stringz import trunc_str trunc_str("hello world", max_chars=10) 'hello w...'

No truncation needed:

trunc_str("short", max_chars=10) 'short'

Custom placeholder:

trunc_str("hello world", max_chars=10, placeholder=">>") 'hello wo>>'

Empty placeholder:

trunc_str("hello world", max_chars=5, placeholder="") 'hello'

def trunc_str(
    text: str,
    max_chars: int,
    placeholder: str = "...",
) -> str:
    """A function that truncates a string to a maximum number of characters,
    appending a placeholder if truncation occurs.

    Example:
        Basic usage:

        >>> from stringz import trunc_str
        >>> trunc_str("hello world", max_chars=10)
        'hello w...'

        No truncation needed:

        >>> trunc_str("short", max_chars=10)
        'short'

        Custom placeholder:

        >>> trunc_str("hello world", max_chars=10, placeholder=">>")
        'hello wo>>'

        Empty placeholder:

        >>> trunc_str("hello world", max_chars=5, placeholder="")
        'hello'

    Args:
        text: The string to be truncated.
        max_chars: The maximum number of characters allowed in the output string.
        placeholder: The string to append if truncation occurs. Default is '...'.

    Returns:
        The truncated string, if necessary, with the placeholder appended.

    Raises:
        TypeError: If text is not a string.
        ValueError: If max_chars is not a positive integer or if placeholder length is greater than or
            equal to max_chars.
        TypeError: If placeholder is not a string.
        ValueError: If placeholder length is greater than or equal to max_chars.
    """

    # ====> VALIDATION
    if not isinstance(text, str):
        _err: str = f"text must be a string, not {type(text).__name__}"
        raise TypeError(_err)
    if not isinstance(max_chars, int) or max_chars <= 0:
        _err: str = f"max_chars must be a positive integer, got {max_chars}"
        raise ValueError(_err)
    if not isinstance(placeholder, str):
        _err: str = f"placeholder must be a string, not {type(placeholder).__name__}"
        raise TypeError(_err)
    if len(placeholder) >= max_chars:
        _err: str = f"placeholder length ({len(placeholder)}) must be smaller than max_chars ({max_chars})"
        raise ValueError(_err)

    # ====> TRUNCATE
    if len(text) <= max_chars:
        return text
    return text[: max_chars - len(placeholder)] + placeholder

items.title: TStr
items.text:
Bases: str

A string subclass that automatically truncates its content to a maximum length when created or modified through string operations. The TStr class uses the trunc_str function for truncation under the hood.

Example

Basic creation:

from stringz import TStr s = TStr("hello world", max_chars=10) print(s) hello w... len(s) 10

String operations maintain TStr type and truncation:

s1 = TStr("hello", max_chars=10) s2 = s1 + " world" type(s2) <class 'stringz._truncated_string.TStr'> print(s2) hello w...

items.title: Truncated Strings
items.text: stringz provides two ways to truncate strings: the trunc_str function for one-off truncation, and the TStr class for strings that stay truncated as you work with them.

items.title: trunc_str
items.text:
trunc_str truncates a string to a maximum number of characters, appending a placeholder when truncation occurs.

from stringz import trunc_str

trunc_str("hello world", max_chars=10)
# 'hello w...'

If the string already fits, it is returned unchanged:

trunc_str("short", max_chars=10)
# 'short'

The placeholder is included in the character budget, and can be customized — or left empty to simply cut the string off:

trunc_str("hello world", max_chars=10, placeholder=">>")
# 'hello wo>>'

trunc_str("hello world", max_chars=5, placeholder="")
# 'hello'

items.title: Validation
items.text:
trunc_str validates its inputs and raises:

  • TypeError if text or placeholder is not a string.
  • ValueError if max_chars is not a positive integer.
  • ValueError if the placeholder is longer than or equal to max_chars — there would be no room left for actual content.

items.title: TStr
items.text:
TStr is a subclass of str that automatically truncates its content to a maximum length — not just when it is created, but whenever string operations produce a new value. It uses trunc_str under the hood.

from stringz import TStr

s = TStr("hello world", max_chars=10)
print(s)        # hello w...
len(s)          # 10

Because TStr is a str, it works anywhere a normal string does. The difference is that operations such as concatenation, repetition, formatting and slicing return new TStr instances that keep the max_chars limit:

s1 = TStr("hello", max_chars=10)
s2 = s1 + " world"

type(s2)        # <class 'stringz.TStr'>
print(s2)       # hello w...

Pass max_chars=None (the default) to disable truncation entirely while still getting a TStr:

s = TStr("hello world")
print(s)        # hello world

The placeholder can be customized as well:

s = TStr("hello world", max_chars=10, placeholder=">>")
print(s)        # hello wo>>

items.title: When to use which
items.text:
• Use trunc_str when you need to shorten a single value once — e.g. trimming text before logging or displaying it.
  • Use TStr when the limit should travel with the value — e.g. a field that must never exceed a column width, even after being concatenated or reformatted.
